lead: A wet solid is not a bucket of water. Water sits in pores, on surfaces and inside cell walls, and part of it is held so tightly that ordinary air cannot pull it out. Drying stops when the solid's moisture equals the equilibrium moisture of the air around it. Engineers use moisture content on a dry basis, equilibrium isotherms and free moisture to judge how much water a dryer can remove and where the drying rate will change. This chapter builds that picture and links it to drying rate curves.
prereq: You need: 7.1 for absolute humidity and 7.2 for relative humidity and the psychrometric chart.

sections.h3: Moisture content on dry and wet bases

blocks.text: A solid sample has mass m<sub>s</sub> of dry solid and m<sub>w</sub> of water. The dry-basis moisture content X is kg water per kg dry solid. The wet-basis moisture w is kg water per kg wet solid. Dryers and drying curves use X because the dry solid mass does not change; buyers and labels often use w.

blocks.where: X is kg water per kg dry solid; m<sub>w</sub> is kg water; m<sub>s</sub> is kg dry solid.
w is kg water per kg wet solid; X is kg water per kg dry solid.

blocks.text: The reverse conversion is X = w/(1 − w). A sample that is 30 % water on a wet basis has w = 0.30 and X = 0.30/0.70 = 0.429 kg/kg dry solid, not 0.30. Keep the basis on every number.

sections.h3: Bound, unbound, free and equilibrium moisture

blocks.text: Bound moisture is held by sorption on surfaces and inside cell walls; it exerts a vapour pressure below that of pure water. Unbound moisture is liquid in large pores and capillaries; it behaves like ordinary water. Free moisture is the water above the equilibrium value, X − X*. Only free moisture can be removed by air of a given state.

blocks.where: X<sub>f</sub> is free moisture, kg/kg dry solid; X is current moisture, kg/kg dry solid; X* is equilibrium moisture, kg/kg dry solid.

blocks.text: Equilibrium moisture content X* is the moisture a solid holds when it neither gains nor loses water to air at a fixed temperature and relative humidity. At X = X*, evaporation and condensation are equal. A perfectly non-hygroscopic solid such as clean sand has X* close to zero at every relative humidity, because its water sits in open pores and escapes as freely as pure water. Hygroscopic solids such as wood, clay and food retain water even in dry air, so X* > 0.

items: Hygroscopic: X* rises steeply near high relative humidity; water is sorbed in cell walls.
Non-hygroscopic: X* is small or zero; water sits in pores.

Hysteresis: the desorption curve lies above the adsorption curve. At the same relative humidity a solid that is being dried holds more water than the same solid taking up water from dry air. A dried solid exposed to humid air follows the lower adsorption branch.

blocks.text: Temperature shifts the isotherm: warmer air gives a lower X* at the same relative humidity. Use the isotherm at the dryer temperature, not a room-temperature curve.
Drying has three resistances in series: movement inside the solid, vapour transport away from the surface, and heat supply to the surface. The slowest step sets the rate.

items: Capillary flow: surface tension pulls water along narrow pores toward the drying surface.
Liquid diffusion: water moves through the solid phase down a concentration gradient.
Vapour diffusion: water evaporates inside the solid and vapour diffuses through pores to the surface.
Surface evaporation: at the interface, water changes to vapour; the surface temperature falls toward the wet-bulb temperature.
Heat and mass transfer: air supplies sensible heat and carries vapour away; the rates depend on air temperature, humidity, velocity and solid thickness.

blocks.text: Early in drying the surface is wet. Capillary flow and surface evaporation keep it saturated, so the rate is nearly constant and controlled by the air. This is the constant-rate period. Later the surface dries, the evaporation front moves inward, and internal diffusion controls the rate. The rate falls as X falls; this is the falling-rate period. 7.7 turns these periods into drying-time calculations.

The constant-rate period ends at the critical moisture content X<sub>c</sub>, in kg water per kg dry solid, where the surface can no longer stay fully wet. The falling-rate period that follows often has two parts: an unsaturated-surface part, where dry patches grow between wet ones, and a part controlled entirely by internal diffusion. A thin solid in fast air may show only the second part.

Thick solids, low air velocity and high air humidity all slow drying. A high air temperature raises surface evaporation but can case-harden food or crack clay; the solid sets the allowable temperature. Surface heat and mass transfer coefficients follow the correlations in Unit 2.

figure.caption: The curve is the equilibrium moisture isotherm. At 40 % relative humidity the solid holds X* = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid, the orange point.

spec.aria: An equilibrium moisture isotherm rising steeply with relative humidity, with an operating point at 40 percent relative humidity where X-star is 0.10.

examples.question: 100 kg of wet solid contains 30 kg of water. It is placed in air at 40 % relative humidity, for which the equilibrium moisture content is 0.10 kg/kg dry solid. Find the moisture on dry and wet bases, the free moisture and the mass of water that can be removed.
steps: Dry-basis moisture X = m<sub>w</sub>/m<sub>s</sub> = 30/70 = 0.4286 = 0.429 kg/kg dry solid.
Free moisture = X − X* = 0.4286 − 0.10 = 0.3286 = 0.329 kg/kg dry solid.
Water left at equilibrium = X* × m<sub>s</sub> = 0.10 × 70 = 7.0 kg.
Water removable = 30 − 7.0 = 23.0 kg, which also equals 0.3286 × 70 = 23.0 kg.
examples.answer: Dry solid is 70 kg; X = 0.429 kg/kg dry solid; wet basis = 30 %; free moisture = 0.329 kg/kg dry solid; 23.0 kg of water can be removed, leaving 7.0 kg.
examples.check:
ms = 100 - 30
mw = 30
X = mw / ms
w = mw / 100
Xstar = 0.10
free = X - Xstar
left = Xstar * ms
removable = mw - left
print(f"{ms:.1f}")
print(f"{X:.3f}")
print(f"{w*100:.1f}")
print(f"{free:.3f}")
print(f"{removable:.1f}")
print(f"{left:.1f}")

traps: Setting X* = 0. At any relative humidity a hygroscopic solid has X* > 0; air cannot dry it to zero.
Swapping bases. A 30 % wet-basis sample has X = 0.429, not 0.30.
Using X − X* when X is on a wet basis. Convert both moisture contents to dry basis first.
Confusing free moisture with unbound moisture. Free is above equilibrium; unbound is pore water.
Using a room-temperature isotherm for a hot dryer. X* falls as temperature rises, and hysteresis matters.

quiz.q: Define dry-basis and wet-basis moisture content, with units.
quiz.a: X = kg water/kg dry solid. w = kg water/kg wet solid. X = w/(1 − w).

quiz.q: Why can air at 40 % relative humidity not dry a hygroscopic solid below X* = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid?
quiz.a: At X* the solid's water has the same escaping tendency as vapour in that air; net evaporation is zero. Below X*, water would be absorbed.

quiz.q: 50 kg of wet solid contains 20 kg of water. Air gives X* = 0.05 kg/kg dry solid. Find X, free moisture and removable water.
Why is the desorption isotherm above the adsorption isotherm?
quiz.a: Desorption sits above adsorption because of pore shape (ink-bottle pores: a wide pore body cannot empty until its narrow neck empties, so during drying the body stays filled down to a lower relative humidity) and because air is trapped in pores during wetting, blocking some sites. So at the same relative humidity the drying path keeps more water and the wetting path keeps less.

quiz.q: Which solids are hygroscopic: sand, wood, clay, food?
quiz.a: Wood, clay and food are hygroscopic; clean sand is nearly non-hygroscopic.

quiz.q: Convert X = 0.25 kg/kg dry solid to wet basis.
What controls the rate in the constant-rate period and in the falling-rate period?
quiz.a: Constant rate: surface evaporation controlled by air temperature, humidity and velocity. Falling rate: internal capillary flow and vapour diffusion control.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial drying of food, wood and pharmaceuticals uses water sorption isotherms to set safe moisture limits and predict shelf life. Research extends the equilibrium curve to multi-component foods and to freeze-drying, where ice sublimation adds a second transport step. Search water sorption isotherm, GAB equation and effective moisture diffusivity to go deeper.
